title: Cheapest Basket With Bundle Deals
statement:
A shop sells n kinds of items. One unit of item i costs prices[i].

The shop also runs bundle deals. Each bundles[j] has n + 1 numbers: the first n say how many units of each item the bundle contains, and the last is the bundle's price. You may buy any bundle as many times as you like.

Your shopping list needs[i] says exactly how many units of item i you want. You must end up with exactly that many of every item: a bundle that would give you more than you need of anything cannot be used. Return the lowest total cost.

examples.why: Second bundle (10) plus two single units of item 0 (4). Using the first bundle instead costs 5 + 10 = 15, and both bundles together overshoot item 0.
The bundle is worse than buying single units, so you ignore it.
The bundle is cheap, but it would give 3 units when you need 2, so it is not allowed.

constraints: bundles[j].length = n + 1, every count 0 … 6, bundle price 0 … 50
Every bundle contains at least one unit
hints: The order in which you buy things does not matter. What does the problem look like after you buy one bundle?
After one purchase you face the same problem with a smaller shopping list. The answer for a shopping list never changes, so cache it.
best(needs) = min(buy everything as single units, and for every bundle that fits: bundle price + best(needs − bundle)). Key the cache on the needs vector.

explain.intuition:
Whatever you buy first, what is left is the same problem with a shorter shopping list. So define best(list) as the cheapest way to fill that list. One option is always to buy every unit on its own. The other options are "take one bundle that fits, then solve the rest", for each bundle.

The same leftover list shows up through many different buying orders (bundle A then B, or B then A). Caching best by the list itself, like memoizing a selector by its input, means each list is solved once. With 6 items and at most 6 of each there are at most 76 lists, and usually far fewer are reachable.
steps: Define best(list). Start with the cost of buying every unit on the list at its single price.
For each bundle, skip it if any of its counts is larger than what the list still needs.
Otherwise subtract the bundle from the list and try bundlePrice + best(rest).
Return the minimum, and store it in a map keyed by the list (for example joined into a string or a tuple).
pitfalls: Using a bundle that overshoots one item. Extra units are not allowed, even when the bundle would be cheaper.
Assuming a bundle is always better than single units. Always keep "buy the rest one by one" as an option.
Greedily using the bundle with the biggest saving first. In the first example the bundle that looks better per unit leads to 15, not 14.

complexity.time: O(S · m · n), S = number of reachable lists, m = bundles

solutions.title: Plain recursion
solutions.idea: Try every bundle that fits, recurse on what is left, and compare against buying the rest as single units. Many leftover lists are solved again and again.

solutions.title: Memoized search on the shopping list
solutions.idea: Same recursion, but cache the answer for each leftover list. Bundles that cost no less than their contents bought singly are dropped up front, since they never help.

followups: Why is it safe to throw away bundles that cost at least as much as their contents?
What if you were allowed to buy more than you need? How does the state space change?
